blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript. The compiler checks your code, then removes the types, so at run time it's plain JavaScript. Most React job postings now expect it. And coming from Java, you'll feel at home quickly, with one big difference.

### Structural typing

Java cares about what a type is called. TypeScript cares about what shape it has.

blocks.title: Same shape, so it's accepted

blocks.text:
There are no `implements` requirements, and two types with the same fields are interchangeable. This fits JavaScript, where objects come from JSON.

### Everyday types

blocks.title: Annotations you'll write daily

blocks.text:
Let inference do the work for local variables, and annotate function parameters and public APIs.

| Java | TypeScript |
|---|---|
| `enum Status { PAID }` | `'PAID' \| 'SHIPPED'`, usually better |
| `Optional<String>` | `string \| undefined` |
| `List<Order>` | `Order[]` |
| `Map<String, Order>` | `Record<string, Order>` or `Map` |
| `Object` | `unknown` (safe) or `any` (unsafe) |
| `T extends Comparable<T>` | `T extends { id: string }` |

### interface or type?

Both describe object shapes. `type` can also express unions and more. Many teams use `interface` for objects and props, and `type` for unions. Pick one convention, and don't spend long on this.

### any and unknown

`any` turns off checking, and it spreads. `unknown` forces you to check before use.

blocks.title: unknown makes you prove it

blocks.text:
### Strict mode

Set `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json`. With `strictNullChecks`, `null` and `undefined` aren't part of every type, which removes the equivalent of Java's `NullPointerException` at compile time.

blocks.title: The compiler catches what Java wouldn't

blocks.text: `const order: Order = await res.json()` is an unverified promise to the compiler. If the API returns something else, TypeScript won't notice. Validate at the boundary with a library such as Zod, where it matters.
blocks.title: Types vanish at run time
Key points
blocks.text:
- Shape matters, not the name
- Turn on strict
- Prefer unknown to any
- Types don't check data at run time

### Narrowing

The compiler tracks your checks, and refines types within each branch.

blocks.title: Control flow narrows the type

blocks.text:
### Discriminated unions

This pattern replaces a lot of Java class hierarchies, and it's perfect for UI states. A shared literal field tells the compiler which variant it has.

blocks.title: Impossible states become impossible

blocks.text: Compare it with `{ loading: boolean; error?: string; data?: T[] }`, which permits nonsense such as loading and error together. Model states so that invalid combinations can't exist.

blocks.title: Exhaustiveness: get an error if a case is forgotten

blocks.text:
### Generics

They work much as in Java, with inference doing most of the work.

blocks.title: A generic API helper

blocks.text:
### Utility types

Transform existing types, rather than repeating them.

| Utility | Meaning | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| `Partial<T>` | All fields optional | PATCH payloads |
| `Required<T>` | All required | Normalised config |
| `Pick<T, 'a' \| 'b'>` | Only these | List rows |
| `Omit<T, 'id'>` | All but these | Create requests |
| `Readonly<T>` | No reassignment | Props |
| `Record<K, V>` | Key-value map | Lookup tables |
| `ReturnType<typeof f>` | A function's return | Reuse without repeating |

blocks.title: Derive types from one source

blocks.title: Deriving a union from a value

blocks.text: Now the list exists at run time for your dropdown, and the type always matches it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Narrow with ordinary checks
- Use discriminated unions for states
- Use utility types rather than repeating
- Derive types from a single source

### Generic components

blocks.title: A reusable list

blocks.text:
### Keeping Java and TypeScript in sync

Your Spring Boot records and TypeScript interfaces describe the same data. Writing both by hand lets them drift.

| Approach | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Handwrite | Copy by hand | Simple, and goes out of date |
| OpenAPI generation | springdoc produces a spec, and `openapi-typescript` generates types | Automatic, needs a build step |
| Zod schemas | Validate at run time, and infer types | Also catches real mismatches |

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Spring Boot controllers and records] --> B[springdoc: openapi.json]
  B --> C[openapi-typescript]
  C --> D[api-types.ts]
  D --> E[React code gets compile errors when the API changes]
blocks.title: Generating types from your API

blocks.text: Now renaming a Java field causes a TypeScript compile error in the frontend, rather than a bug in production. It's a strong point for a full stack interview.

blocks.title: Runtime validation with Zod

blocks.text:
### Mapping Java types to JSON

| Java | JSON | TypeScript | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| `long` | number | `number` | Loses precision: send as a string when large |
| `BigDecimal` | number or string | `string` | Prefer a string for money |
| `LocalDate` | `"2026-10-31"` | `string` | Not a `Date` until you parse it |
| `Instant` | `"2026-10-31T10:15:30Z"` | `string` | Parse, and watch timezones |
| `Optional`, nullable | value or `null` | `T \| null` | `null`, not `undefined` |
| `enum` | `"PAID"` | a union | Keep in sync |

### Compiler settings

blocks.title: A sensible tsconfig excerpt

blocks.text: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes `items[0]` possibly undefined, matching reality. Vite doesn't type-check, so run `tsc --noEmit` in CI.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Type props with interfaces
- Generate types from OpenAPI to keep Java and TS in sync
- A JSON date is a string
- Run tsc in CI

You don't need type gymnastics to do daily work, but you'll read these in library code and error messages.

### Type guards

A function can teach the compiler what a check proves.

blocks.title: A user-defined type guard

blocks.text: `filter` also narrows with a guard:

blocks.code:
const raw: (string | null)[] = ['a', null, 'b'];
const clean = raw.filter((x): x is string => x !== null);   // string[]
blocks.title: Removing nulls from an array

blocks.text:
Be careful: the compiler trusts a guard without checking it, so a wrong guard gives you confident wrong types.

### Mapped types

These transform every property of a type. It's how `Partial` is built.

blocks.title: Mapped types

blocks.title: Strongly typed strings

blocks.text:
### satisfies

`satisfies` checks a value against a type, while keeping its specific inferred type.

blocks.title: satisfies keeps the detail

blocks.text: ### Function overloads and generics with constraints

blocks.title: Constraints

blocks.text:
### Reading long error messages

TypeScript errors can run many lines. Read from the **bottom up**, since the last line usually states the real mismatch. For example: "Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'number'" at the end of a long form error tells you exactly which field differs.

### Don't overdo it

| Reasonable | Probably too much |
|---|---|
| Unions, generics with one or two parameters | Recursive conditional types in app code |
| `Pick`, `Omit`, `Partial` | Types nobody on the team can read |
| A type guard at a boundary | `as` everywhere to silence errors |

`as` tells the compiler to trust you, and it's the usual way that types and reality drift apart. Use it rarely, and never `as any`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Guards teach narrowing, but aren't checked
- Mapped types transform every field
- satisfies keeps specific types
- Read long errors from the bottom

sections.title: Modelling a real API in TypeScript

blocks.text: ### A worked example: paged orders

blocks.title: Types for a Spring Data response

blocks.text:
### DTOs and view models

The server's shape isn't always what your screen needs. Convert once at the edge, rather than parsing dates in every component.

blocks.title: A mapper at the boundary
Use it with a query's select

blocks.text:
### Exhaustive mapping

`Record` makes the compiler enforce completeness. Add a new status, and the build fails here until you handle it, a benefit Java gets from `switch` on sealed types.

blocks.title: A label for every status

blocks.text:
### Branded types

Structural typing means that a `userId` string can be passed where an `orderId` string belongs. A brand prevents this.

blocks.title: Stop mixing up IDs

blocks.text:
It exists only at compile time. Use it where mix-ups would be costly.

### Environment variables

blocks.title: Validate configuration at start-up

blocks.text:
A clear start-up failure beats a mysterious runtime bug.

### Moving JavaScript to TypeScript

1. Add `tsconfig.json` with `allowJs: true`, so that both work together.
2. Rename files one at a time, starting with small utility modules with no dependencies.
3. Add types at boundaries first: API responses, then props.
4. Allow `any` temporarily, marked with a comment.
5. Turn on `strict`, then fix what appears, in stages.

Don't rewrite everything at once. A gradual path keeps features shipping, the same way you'd migrate a legacy Java module.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Convert DTOs at the edge
- Record forces handling every case
- Brands stop ID mix-ups
- Migrate gradually
#### TypeScript for Java developers

items.question: Why does an object with extra fields satisfy an interface?
items.answer: Typing is structural: it only needs the required fields. (Fresh object literals get an extra check for typos.)

items.question: Does TypeScript validate an API response at run time?
items.answer: No. Types are removed in compilation. Use a validator such as Zod at the boundary.

items.question: What's the difference between any and unknown?
items.answer: `any` turns off checks. `unknown` allows anything in, but requires checks before use.

blocks.text: #### Narrowing, unions and generics

items.question: Why is a status union better than three booleans for loading, error and success?
items.answer: Booleans permit impossible combinations. A union allows exactly one state, with the right data.

items.question: What does Partial<Order> give you?
items.answer: A type with all of Order's fields optional, useful for updates.

items.question: Why can a generic getJson<Order[]> still be wrong at run time?
items.answer: The cast promises a shape with no check. Validate the data if you need certainty.

blocks.text: #### TypeScript with React and your API

items.question: Your frontend treats order.createdAt as a Date and crashes. Why?
items.answer: JSON has no date type, so it's a string. Parse it explicitly.

items.question: How can a backend rename cause a frontend compile error?
items.answer: Generate TypeScript types from the OpenAPI spec, so a renamed field breaks the type check.

items.question: Vite builds fine, but the code has a type error. Why?
items.answer: Vite strips types without checking them. Run `tsc --noEmit` separately, in CI.

blocks.text: #### Advanced types you'll actually meet

items.question: Why might a type guard be dangerous?
items.answer: The compiler trusts it. If its logic is wrong, your types are wrong with no warning.

items.question: What does `as const` differ from `satisfies` in?
items.answer: `as const` makes literal, readonly types. `satisfies` checks against a type without widening.

items.question: Where do you start with a long TypeScript error?
items.answer: At the bottom line, which usually names the real mismatch.

blocks.text: #### Modelling a real API in TypeScript

items.question: Why convert API data in one place?
items.answer: Components then get ready-to-use values, and date or money parsing isn't repeated or missed.

items.question: You add a new OrderStatus. How can the compiler find what needs updating?
items.answer: Exhaustive `Record<OrderStatus, ...>` maps and never-checks produce errors until each case is handled.

items.question: Why send BigDecimal as a string?
items.answer: Converting to a JavaScript number can lose precision. A string keeps the exact value.
